steps.title: ICP and Market Size
steps.summary: Who we are talking to, and how big the opportunity is.
steps.paragraph: “Chanchal mann, ati random” (a restless mind, very random) describes how a woman feels through her cycle, and how her generation lives: always switching between things. Ayni is built for that woman. We are predominantly targeting women in tier-1 cities, and Parul’s brief names Gen Z and young urban consumers as the core audience. Within that group, our segments are Gen Z with generous pocket money, fitness enthusiasts, swimmers, dancers, new mothers and women with urinary incontinence. Each wants a period product that keeps up with her day, and wants proof that it is comfortable, leak-safe and easy to look after. The college interviews are a first step with the Gen Z segment, and I’d add the other segments next.
steps.insight: Her words, not ours, should write the captions.

Market size will be built from public sources: the number of menstruating women in the target region, current usage of disposable products, and the share open to reusable alternatives.
steps.market: The category is small in India and growing. Global reusable period underwear is estimated at about USD 280M in 2025, rising to about USD 868M by 2033 (Grand View Research). India’s share is far smaller, with one report putting it at USD 4.2M in 2022 and USD 17.3M by 2030, and other reports giving different figures. About 89% of urban women aged 15 to 24 already use hygienic period products (NFHS-5 analysis), so the opportunity is switching from disposables.

steps.title: Business goals to social goals to KPIs
steps.summary: Turning what the business needs into what social media measures.
steps.paragraph:
Before posting anything, I’d connect each business goal to one social goal and a few measurable KPIs, so every piece of content has a job. For a brand that hasn’t launched, the goals are to become known, build a waitlist, and be ready to convert people when the product goes on sale. Before launch, the number that matters isn’t sales. It’s how many people raise their hand to hear more. Likes are not the measure. Saves, shares, DMs, waitlist sign-ups and link clicks are, because they show intent.

Awareness comes first. In my college interviews, many women had never heard of period underwear. Those who had were hesitant for two reasons: they thought wearing it for hours would be unhygienic, and they thought washing it would be a hassle. So the first goal is simply to make the product known. The second is to answer those two objections with clear, expert-backed content before anyone is asked to buy. That is why the early KPIs are reach, shares, saves and waitlist sign-ups. Those numbers show that people have noticed Ayni and want to know more.

People come to Instagram to be entertained and educated, in a playful way, so my goal here is to build curiosity. Two of these pieces explain what period underwear is and answer the doubts from my interviews. The other two are shareable videos built on the Y2K nostalgia Gen Z loves.
steps.insight: Fewer KPIs, tied to a decision, beat a long dashboard.

steps.title: Competitor analysis and insights
steps.summary: What the two main Indian players do, and where Ayni can stand apart.
steps.paragraph: I looked at the two leading Indian period underwear brands, Mahina and HealthFab, and one indirect competitor, Nua. HealthFab’s social presence is functional but not very visually engaging. Mahina does it better: it mixes aesthetic photo campaigns with educational content, and it dominates organic search, ranking first on Google for “period underwear”. Mahina began posting on 11 September 2023 but wasn’t consistent until 2025. In 2025 it ran a lot of influencer marketing, and its reach grew sharply after that. Nua competes for the same shopper from the wider menstrual wellness side, with heavy investment in commercial ads. The lesson for Ayni is to be consistent from day one, to seed creators early, and to take the space none of them owns: humour that looks as good as it sounds.

steps.title: Content strategy
steps.summary: Content for the top, middle and bottom of the funnel.
steps.paragraph: I’d plan content across the funnel, which is how a stranger becomes a customer. Top of the funnel is awareness: playful, shareable content that makes her curious. Middle is trust and community: education, behind the scenes, and answers to the doubts from my interviews, such as whether period underwear is hygienic and whether it is a hassle to wash. Because Ayni positions itself as a lifestyle brand, not a period-care brand, I’d also run interview campaigns, visiting colleges and talking to young women about wider topics in their lives, not only periods. These put real voices on the page, make Ayni part of her world, and give us language to use in captions. Bottom is conversion: product demos, FAQs and the waitlist. Because Ayni is launching, the mix shifts over time. Before launch it leans towards awareness, since few people know the brand or the category. At launch it leans towards conversion, with something like 40% top, 20% middle and 40% bottom as a starting point. After launch it settles into a balance, with community and customer stories added once they exist. Before the product is on sale, bottom-of-funnel content means waitlist sign-ups, product reveals and answering buying questions, not “buy now”.
steps.insight: Humour opens the door, product proof closes it.

steps.title: Engagement strategy
steps.summary: How Ayni talks with its community, not just at it.
steps.paragraph:
At launch, I want to talk to everyone who comes to Ayni’s page. If someone comments, DMs, replies to a story or shares a post, I’ll reply, myself. At that stage there aren’t many people, so it’s doable, and it’s the best way to hear what they actually ask and how they talk. Anything about health goes to Baala’s experts. Once there are too many messages, I’ll set up saved replies for the common questions, but I’ll still handle anything personal by hand.

I’d also keep an organic presence on Twitter (X). It skews male, but men are customers too: they buy for partners, sisters and mothers, and they recommend what they trust. Showing up there in a respectful, informative voice puts Ayni in front of a group that most period brands overlook.
steps.insight: Every comment is a chance to sound like a friend.
